description: Presentation rules for the customer-facing weekly Excel workbook. This file decides how an internal opportunity is described to a subscriber's sales team: which plain-English priority it carries, how its goods list is compressed to something readable, and which commercial angle suits the supplier reading it. It changes wording and layout only. It never touches the LaunchTrace Score, qualification, entity matching or buying-intent classification.
usage_note: Every sentence produced from this file must be supportable by what is already stored on the opportunity. Angles are suggestions for how a supplier might approach a brand, never claims that the brand has asked for anything.

priority.note: A customer-facing priority, specific to the supplier reading the workbook. TOP MATCH means one of the strongest opportunities FOR THIS CUSTOMER this week — the operator-approved selection where one exists, otherwise the best of the supplier-specific matches by fit. It deliberately does not mean 'has a HIGH internal band': a generically strong launch signal in a category this supplier barely serves is not one of their best leads. STRONG and RELEVANT split the remaining qualified matches on the same supplier fit the matcher already computed. Nothing here reorders, promotes or admits a lead that did not qualify on its own merit, and no underlying score or band is changed or shown.

levels.meaning: One of the strongest opportunities for you this week. Start here.
A clear early-stage brand in a category you serve. Worth a call this week.
Qualified and in scope, but a partial fit. Read the angle before spending time on it.

priority.default_top_match_note: How many leads carry TOP MATCH when no approved selection exists for the week. Taken from the top of the supplier-specific fit order, never from the internal band.

category_short_labels.note: Short names for the same categories, used where a full taxonomy label would make a sentence unreadable.

product_summary.note: Turns a trade mark goods list into one readable line. A head is used only when its keyword appears in the stored goods text, and a format is listed only when its keyword appears too, so the line is always a compression of the real filing rather than a description of it. A format that merely repeats a word from the head is dropped as noise, unless keep_with_head marks it as a real format in its own right (coffee bags, tea bags).

supplier_angles.note: One relevance sentence and one suggested angle per product category, written for the supplier profile reading the workbook. {brand} and {product} are filled from the opportunity. The angle is a suggestion about how this supplier might approach the brand, never a statement about what the brand wants.

_default.relevance: An early-stage UK food brand that has recently filed a trade mark application, in a category where printed film or pouches are part of the pack.
_default.angle: Short-run printed film for the range as it comes to market.

coffee_tea.relevance: {product_head} is a printed-pouch category. Film and bag formats are normally the first pack decision a hot-drinks brand makes, and usually across several SKUs at once.

angle.Coffee: Short-run printed coffee pouches across multiple SKUs, with drip-bag and coffee-bag film as a natural second format.
angle.Tea: Small-batch printed tea pouches, with digital print keeping the quantity per SKU low.

snacks.relevance: {product_head} go to market in printed bags and pouches. A range with several variants means several designs, each at modest volume.

angle.Nuts: Resealable printed pouches for the nut and snack-mix range — one short run per flavour rather than one long run.
angle.Vegetable crisps and fries: Printed snack bags across the crisp variants, with frozen-suitable film for the fry lines.
angle._default: Flexible snack packaging for the new range, at launch quantities rather than full production runs.

cereal_bars.relevance: {product_head} are flow-wrapped, so wrapper film and artwork are part of getting a first production run onto shelf.
cereal_bars.angle: First-run bar wrappers — flow-wrap film at launch quantities.

confectionery.relevance: {product_head} uses printed film, flow-wrap and pouches. A range that pairs sweets with other merchandise usually carries several small formats rather than one.
confectionery.angle: Short-run printed film and pouches across a multi-SKU confectionery range, where no single line justifies a long run.

chilled_frozen.relevance: {product_head} is mostly pots and labels rather than film. The granola, frozen and lidding formats in the same filing are the part that is flexible-pack work.
chilled_frozen.angle: Lower priority for film. Worth a call if the granola or frozen lines come first, or for lidding and sleeve work alongside the chilled range.

sauces_condiments.relevance: {product_head} reach shelf in glass or in pouches and sachets. Where a brand chooses pouches, it is flexible-pack work from the first batch onwards.
sauces_condiments.angle: Printed pouches and sachets for the range — worth asking whether they have settled on glass or pouch before pitching a format.

stage_clause.note: Appended to the relevance line so two brands in the same category do not read identically. Says what the public evidence shows about how far the brand has got. It must never imply we know whether a supplier has been chosen, a pack format settled, or a purchase committed — we have no visibility of any of that.
stage_clause.selling_direct: The brand is already trading, so this may be more relevant as a range-extension, alternative-supplier or short-run conversation.
stage_clause.no_website: We could not confirm a brand website, so there is less public evidence about how far the launch has progressed.
stage_clause.pre_launch: There is little public evidence about the brand so far, so an early introduction is more about being known to them than about any specific project.

copy.what_this_is: LaunchTrace reads the UK Intellectual Property Office trade mark journal every week, matches each food and drink applicant to Companies House, and keeps only the brands that look genuinely early-stage. This brief covers the opportunities from that week that are relevant to what {customer} sells. Every company here has recently filed a UK trade mark application for a brand or product range; none of them has been contacted, and none has asked to be introduced to a supplier.
copy.top_section_note: The full list, with filters and space for your own notes, is on the OPPORTUNITIES tab.
copy.angle_disclaimer: Suggested sales angles are LaunchTrace's view of how you might approach each brand. They are a suggested approach, not evidence of current buying intent, and not a request, enquiry or stated requirement.
copy.footer: Sources: UK Intellectual Property Office Trade Marks Journal and Companies House, under the Open Government Licence v3.0. Commercial signals, not confirmed buying intent.

how_to_use.heading: What LaunchTrace detects
how_to_use.body: Every week the UK Intellectual Property Office publishes the trade mark applications that have been filed. A new food or drink brand almost always files an application for its name before it goes on sale. Publication means the application has been filed and advertised, not that registration is complete. LaunchTrace reads that journal, works out which applicants are real UK food businesses, checks them against Companies House, and keeps only the ones that look like they are still building rather than already established. What you get is a list of brands early enough in their life to be worth introducing yourself to.

how_to_use.heading: What "Why now" means
how_to_use.body: It is the timing evidence: when the application was filed and published, how recently the company behind it was formed, whether this is the first mark we have seen from them, and whether the brand has a website or retailer listings yet. It explains why this week is a sensible moment to make contact, rather than six months from now. It does not tell you anything about who they buy from, or what they have already ordered — we have no visibility of that.

how_to_use.heading: A lead is a signal, not an enquiry
how_to_use.body: Nobody on this list has contacted you, asked for a quote, or been told about you. These are companies whose public filings show a brand being built. Treat every row as a well-timed reason to introduce yourself, not as an inbound enquiry. Nothing here is a confirmed buying request.

how_to_use.heading: How to use the suggested sales angle
how_to_use.body: The angle is our read on what a supplier like you might be able to offer a brand at this stage. It is a starting point for a first conversation — a sensible opening line and a reason to call — not a statement that the company has asked for that product, and not evidence that any supplier decision is still open. Check it against what you actually see on their website or filing before you use it.

how_to_use.heading: Why some websites say "Not confirmed"
how_to_use.body: We only publish a website when we can prove it belongs to that company. If a search turns up a page that might be the brand but might equally be a similarly named business elsewhere, we leave the field as Not confirmed rather than send you to the wrong company. It is usually worth a quick search of your own — the absence of a confirmed site is often a sign the brand is genuinely early.

how_to_use.heading: How to read Priority
how_to_use.body: TOP MATCH — one of the strongest opportunities for you this week. Start here. STRONG — a clear early-stage brand in a category you serve; worth a call this week. RELEVANT — qualified and in scope, but a partial fit; read the suggested angle before spending time on it. Priority is specific to your business, not a general ranking: it weighs how early-stage the brand looks together with how closely what it is launching matches what you sell. A brand can be an unusually strong launch signal in general and still not be one of your best leads, and Priority reflects your side of that.

how_to_use.heading: Working the list
how_to_use.body: The OPPORTUNITIES tab is a filterable table. Sort or filter by Priority, Product Category or Location to split the week between your team, then use the Owner, Sales Status and Sales Notes columns to track what happens. Those three columns are yours — LaunchTrace never writes to them, so your notes survive from week to week if you keep the file.
